title: Circumcision and the sacraments show precepts may lack intrinsic light; God's authority is the chief ground
source_text: XXX. Quum vero Israelitae in Aegypto docerentur marem omnem octavo die esse circumcidendum, a sanguine abstinendum esse, quibusdam animalibus vesci licere, aliis non licere, et plura hujusmodi, nemo negare potest quin ista illis fide amplectenda fuerint, ut res Deo gratae et acceptae. Et tamen quis sincere et ex animo affirmare possit ista in se lucem habuisse, qua sufficienter fidem sui facerent, et unde mens fidelium efficaciter compelleretur ut crederet haec a Deo jussa et tradita fuisse. Idemque hodie nostri respectu, dici potest de lavacro illo aquae quod in Baptismo usurpatur, et de sumptione panis et vini in mensa Domini. Cum igitur fide suscipienda sint dogmata, et praecepta multa, quae non eam in se habent lucem et evidentiam, qua se satis certo vera esse comprobent et a Deo tradita, manifestum est fidei, qua res verbo Dei traditas et religionis dogmata suscipimus, rationem et basin praecipuam, non esse ipsam rei veritatem atque evidentiam, sed potius veritatem et authoritatem Dei docentis et revelantis.
pass_a_gloss: But when the Israelites in Egypt were taught that every male was to be circumcised on the eighth day, that they were to abstain from blood, that it was lawful to eat certain animals and not lawful to eat others, and more things of this kind, no one can deny that those things were to be embraced by them with faith, as things pleasing and acceptable to God. And yet who could sincerely and from the heart affirm that those things had in themselves a light by which they would sufficiently make faith in themselves, and from which the mind of believers would be effectively compelled to believe that these things had been commanded and handed down by God. And the same, with respect to us today, can be said of that washing of water which is used in Baptism, and of the taking of bread and wine at the Lord's table. Since therefore many dogmas and precepts are to be taken up by faith which do not have in themselves that light and evidence by which they would prove themselves with sufficient certainty to be true and handed down by God, it is manifest that the principal ground and basis of the faith by which we take up the things handed down in God's Word and the dogmas of religion is not the very truth and evidence of the thing, but rather the truth and authority of God teaching and revealing.
pass_b_english: When the Israelites in Egypt were taught that every male was to be circumcised on the eighth day, that they were to abstain from blood, that some animals might be eaten and others not, and more of that kind, no one can deny those things were to be embraced by them with faith, as things pleasing and acceptable to God. Yet who could sincerely and from the heart say those things had in themselves a light enough to make faith, and enough to compel believers' minds to conclude that God had commanded and handed them down? The same can be said of us today about that washing of water used in Baptism, and about taking bread and wine at the Lord's table.

So when many dogmas and precepts must be taken up by faith, though they do not have in themselves the light and evidence by which they would prove themselves with enough certainty true and handed down by God, it is clear that the principal ground and basis of the faith by which we take up what God's Word delivers and religion's dogmas is not the thing's own truth and evidence, but rather the truth and authority of God teaching and revealing.
